title: The Sad King and His Book of Games
body: King Alfonso the Tenth of Spain had a very sad end to his reign, with his own family rebelling against him and his kingdom falling into war. During these incredibly stressful times, the king found comfort in art and games. He ended up commissioning one of the most famous medieval books about chess, proving that a board game can offer a peaceful escape from real-world chaos.

To find a quiet space in his mind, he turned to the beautiful, carved shapes of chess pieces. He asked his scribes to paint a magnificent book filled with pictures of people playing games together. It was his way of finding a little bit of peace when the world outside was so loud.

Instead of panicking during the chaos, he made a brilliant, unexpected move. He gathered artists to write one of the greatest game books in history, packed with chess secrets. He showed everyone that even when your kingdom is messy, you can still master the board!

The game was designed to show off a king's supreme power and strike fear into his rivals.

title: Cornering the Hare
body: Long ago, people played a board game called corner the hare. One player controlled a single piece representing a fast hare, while the other player had twelve pieces trying to surround it. If the hare managed to capture enough attackers to leave them with only nine, the hare won. With only nine pieces left, the hunter could no longer trap the clever animal.

If the clever hare could slip past and take three of those pieces away, it won its freedom. With only nine pursuers left on the board, there was simply too much open space for the hare to ever be caught.
variants.luca: Imagine being one lone player facing an army of twelve hunters closing in from every side! This medieval game was a thrilling race where you had to dodge, weave, and strike back. variants.luca: Imagine a guide so packed with brilliant strategies that players across Europe scrambled to get their hands on it! To learn his winning style, rivals rushed to translate the pages into French and Italian. This grand chess adventure lasted for centuries before the complete book was finally printed in English!

title: A Clever Trick to Reach the Prince
body: Back in 1561, a Spanish priest named Ruy López wrote a book about chess. He wanted the young prince of Spain, who loved chess, to read it. To make sure the prince saw it, Ruy López cleverly dedicated the book to the prince's personal teacher!

variants.lucy: Long ago in the year 1561, a Spanish priest named Ruy López wrote down his favorite chess secrets in a special book. He hoped a young prince who adored the game would get to read his quiet pages. To make sure the book found its way into the royal palace, he wrote a lovely dedication to the prince's own teacher.
variants.luca: Ruy López had a brilliant plan to get his new chess book to Spain's young prince! He knew the royal kid loved chess, but getting a book into a palace was a tough mission. So, he pulled a clever move and dedicated the book to the prince's personal teacher instead. That way, the teacher would definitely show the book to his royal student!

title: The Duke's Secret Chess Name
body: In 1616, a German duke named Augustus wanted to publish a translation of a famous chess book. Instead of using his royal name, he made up a secret pen name, Gustavus Selenus, to sign his work.

variants.luca: Imagine a powerful ruler sneaking around to write a book! Duke Augustus wanted to share a legendary chess guide, but he needed a brilliant disguise. He cooked up a secret identity, Gustavus Selenus, and slipped it onto the cover like a spy on a mission.

title: A Prince's Passion for Chess
body: In the sixteenth century, a Spanish priest named Ruy Lopez noticed that young Prince Charles was absolutely crazy about playing chess. Inspired by the prince's great love for the game, the priest decided to write one of the very first complete chess books in history to help people learn how to play.

variants.lucy: Long ago in Spain, a gentle priest named Ruy Lopez watched a young prince named Charles play chess with quiet focus. The prince loved the wooden pieces and the clever squares so much that it touched the priest's heart. To share this joy, the priest sat down and wrote one of the very first guidebooks, filled with secrets to help everyone learn the game.
variants.luca: Imagine a real-life prince from the old days who was totally obsessed with conquering the chessboard! title: A Royal Shield for Ruy Lopez
body: In the sixteenth century, a Spanish priest named Ruy Lopez wrote an important book about chess. To protect his hard work, King Philip the Second granted him a special ten-year monopoly. Back then, book laws were so strict that anyone who copied a book without permission could face massive fines or even the death penalty!

variants.lucy: Long ago in Spain, a gentle priest named Ruy Lopez spent many quiet hours writing down his favorite chess secrets in a special book. To keep this treasure safe, the king himself promised that no one else could print the book for ten whole years. It was like a royal shield made of paper and ink, protecting the priest's hard work.
variants.luca: But watch out, because copying that book without permission was an incredibly dangerous move back then! title: A Royal Guard for a Chess Book
body: Back in the sixteenth century, writing a chess book was a very big deal. The King of Spain himself signed a special decree to protect Ruy López's new chess guide. Anyone who dared to copy or disobey this royal order faced a massive fine of twenty thousand coins, which would be worth a fortune today.

title: The Priest Who Defended Chess Books
body: In the sixteenth century, critics argued that writing a chess guide was pointless because the game had too many possibilities to ever teach. The Spanish priest Ruy López strongly disagreed with this mindset. He argued that just as a fertile field needs cultivation to grow crops, a chess player needs deep study to handle any unexpected moves an opponent might try.

variants.lucy: A long time ago, people thought it was impossible to write a guide for chess because the game has endless paths. A Spanish priest named Ruy López disagreed, believing that a player's mind is like a quiet, empty field. Just as a farmer cares for the soil to help crops grow, he believed we must study to prepare our minds for any surprise.
variants.luca: Imagine being told that chess has too many wild moves to ever write down in a guide! That is what people believed in the 1500s, but a brave priest named Ruy López refused to back down. He argued that you have to prepare your mind like a farmer works the land, getting it ready for action. By studying hard, you can stand strong against any unexpected move your opponent throws at you!

title: Ruy López and the Poisonous Snakes
body: When the famous Spanish priest Ruy López wrote his chess book, he was terrified of jealous rivals. In his introduction, he compared his critics to poisonous snakes waiting to bite him. To protect himself, he dedicated his book to a powerful nobleman, hoping his patron's high status would act as a shield against the haters.

But he worried that other players might be unkind about his work, comparing their harsh words to hidden, biting serpents. To keep his mind at peace, he asked a very important nobleman to protect his beautiful book.
